questions.subject: English Language
questions.text:
Mobile banking has transformed the way millions of Nigerians, particularly those in rural communities, manage their money. Before the spread of mobile money agents and banking apps, many rural dwellers had to travel long distances to the nearest bank branch, often losing an entire day's income in the process. Today, a farmer can receive payment for produce, pay school fees, or transfer money to relatives in another state within seconds, using nothing more than a basic mobile phone. Advocates say this financial inclusion has reduced the amount of cash people must carry, lowering the risk of theft, and has made it easier for small traders to save and access credit. Critics, however, warn that poor network coverage in some remote areas, coupled with the persistent threat of fraud, still discourages many older and less literate users from fully trusting the new technology. Until connectivity improves nationwide and digital literacy spreads further, mobile banking's promise will remain only partly fulfilled for Nigeria's rural poor.

According to the passage, what did rural dwellers often have to do before mobile banking became widespread?
options: Travel long distances to the nearest bank branch
Deposit all their money with the village head
Refuse to use any form of currency
Wait for annual visits from bank officials
questions.explanation: The passage states rural dwellers 'had to travel long distances to the nearest bank branch, often losing an entire day's income in the process.'

What is the closest meaning of the word 'fraud' as used in the passage?
options: A type of mobile phone network
questions.explanation: 'Fraud' refers to wrongful or criminal deception intended to result in financial gain, fitting the context of a threat to mobile banking users.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the option that best completes the sentence: 'Neither the manager nor the staff ___ aware of the new policy.'
questions.explanation: When 'neither...nor' joins a singular and a plural subject, the verb agrees with the nearer subject, 'the staff' (plural), so 'were' is correct.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the underlined word: 'The lecturer's argument was remarkably COGENT.'
questions.explanation: 'Cogent' means clear, logical, and convincing, making 'convincing' the closest synonym.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the option opposite in meaning to the underlined word: 'The twins bore a STRIKING resemblance to each other.'
questions.explanation: 'Striking' means very noticeable; its opposite is 'negligible', meaning too small or unimportant to be worth considering.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correctly spelt word.
questions.explanation: 'Accommodate' is correctly spelt with double 'c' and double 'm'; the other options misspell the word.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the option that best completes the sentence: 'If it ___ tomorrow, the field trip will be cancelled.'
questions.explanation: This is a first conditional describing a real future possibility, which requires the simple present tense in the if-clause: 'if it rains.'

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correct preposition to complete the sentence: 'The students are responsible ___ their own conduct.'
questions.explanation: 'Responsible for' is the standard prepositional pairing used to describe accountability for something.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Identify the part of speech of the underlined word: 'The GENTLY flowing river calmed everyone who watched it.'
questions.explanation: 'Gently' modifies the verb form 'flowing', describing how the river flows, making it an adverb.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the option that is the correct plural form of 'criterion'.
questions.explanation: 'Criterion', derived from Greek, forms its plural irregularly as 'criteria'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the idiom: 'The new employee decided to BITE THE BULLET and confront her difficult colleague.'
options: Report the matter to the police
Face a difficult situation with courage
questions.explanation: 'Bite the bullet' is an idiom meaning to face a painful or difficult situation with resolve and courage.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the option that correctly completes the sentence: 'Mathematics ___ taught in every secondary school in Nigeria.'
questions.explanation: Although 'mathematics' ends in 's', it is treated as a singular subject when referring to the academic discipline, requiring 'is'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the word that best completes the sentence: 'Her ___ comments during the debate impressed the judges.'
questions.explanation: 'Incisive' means showing keen judgement and sharp analysis, fitting the context of impressive comments during a debate.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correctly punctuated sentence.
options: The examination covered three subjects, English Mathematics and Biology.
The examination covered three subjects English, Mathematics, and Biology.
The examination covered three subjects; English, Mathematics, and Biology.
The examination covered three subjects: English, Mathematics, and Biology.
questions.explanation: A colon correctly introduces the list of three subjects following a complete independent clause.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the option that best completes the sentence: 'The information he provided ___ inaccurate.'
questions.explanation: 'Information' is an uncountable noun that takes a singular verb, so 'was inaccurate' is correct.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Identify the figure of speech used: 'The classroom was a zoo during the power outage.'
questions.explanation: This sentence directly equates 'the classroom' with 'a zoo' without using 'like' or 'as', making it a metaphor.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the underlined word: 'The company's expansion plans were remarkably AMBITIOUS.'
questions.explanation: 'Ambitious' describes plans that are highly aspirational or reach for great achievement.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correct form of the verb: 'Each of the candidates ___ given equal time to speak.'
questions.explanation: 'Each' is grammatically singular, so it takes the singular verb 'was', regardless of the plural noun ('candidates') that follows.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the option that best completes the sentence: 'This is the laboratory ___ equipment was recently upgraded.'
questions.explanation: 'Whose' is the possessive relative pronoun correctly used to link 'the laboratory' to 'its equipment.'

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the word opposite in meaning to the underlined word: 'The final decision was entirely ARBITRARY.'
questions.explanation: 'Arbitrary' means based on random choice rather than reason; its opposite is 'reasoned', meaning based on logical thought.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correct option to complete the sentence: 'He is not only intelligent ___ also very hardworking.'
questions.explanation: The correlative pairing 'not only...but also' is the standard grammatical construction used to link two related points.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Identify the correctly spelt word.
questions.explanation: 'Necessary' is correctly spelt with one 'c' and double 's'; the other options are misspellings.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the option that best completes the sentence: 'It was he who ___ appointed team leader.'
questions.explanation: The subject 'he' requires the singular past tense verb 'was' for grammatical agreement.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the underlined word: 'The panel gave a very METICULOUS review of the proposal.'
questions.explanation: 'Meticulous' means showing great attention to detail and being very careful and precise.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correct option: 'The award was presented to my colleague and ___.'
questions.explanation: After a preposition-like construction ('to'), the objective case pronoun 'me' is correct, not the subjective 'I'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the option that correctly completes the sentence: 'The number of applicants ___ increased significantly this year.'
questions.explanation: 'The number of' (referring to a specific total) takes a singular verb, unlike 'a number of', which takes a plural verb.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the option that best expresses the meaning of the sentence: 'The manager decided to TURN A BLIND EYE to the minor infraction.'
questions.explanation: 'Turn a blind eye' is an idiom meaning to deliberately ignore or pretend not to notice something.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the word that is nearest in meaning to the underlined word: 'The old building was found in a state of severe DECREPITUDE.'
options: Disrepair caused by age or neglect
questions.explanation: 'Decrepitude' refers to a state of being worn out or weakened by age or neglect.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correct sentence.
options: Every one of the students has submitted his assignment.
Every one of the students have submitted his assignment.
Every one of the students has submitted they assignment.
Every one of the students have submitted their assignment.
questions.explanation: 'Every one' is grammatically singular, so it correctly takes the singular verb 'has' and singular possessive 'his' in traditional formal usage.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the underlined word: 'The minister's speech was full of PLATITUDES.'
questions.explanation: A 'platitude' is a remark that is trite and overused, often lacking original thought.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the underlined word: 'The old man was known for his TACITURN nature.'
questions.explanation: 'Taciturn' describes a person who is reserved and habitually says little.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the underlined word: 'The evidence presented was deemed CONCLUSIVE by the court.'
questions.explanation: 'Conclusive' evidence is decisive, serving to settle an issue beyond doubt.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the underlined word: 'The professor's explanation was quite LUCID.'
questions.explanation: 'Lucid' means expressed clearly, so a lucid explanation is easy to understand.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the underlined word: 'The negotiations reached an IMPASSE.'
options: A deadlock with no progress possible
questions.explanation: An 'impasse' is a situation in which no progress can be made, a deadlock.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the underlined word: 'Her conduct throughout the crisis was EXEMPLARY.'
questions.explanation: 'Exemplary' means so good that it serves as a desirable model for others.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the underlined word: 'The committee's decision was UNANIMOUS.'
questions.explanation: A 'unanimous' decision is one on which everyone involved is in complete agreement.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the underlined word: 'He gave a CANDID account of what happened.'
questions.explanation: 'Candid' means truthful and straightforward, often about something that may be uncomfortable.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the underlined word: 'The politician's promises were largely SPURIOUS.'
questions.explanation: 'Spurious' means false or fake, not being what it purports to be.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the underlined word: 'The results of the experiment were AMBIGUOUS.'
options: Open to more than one interpretation
questions.explanation: 'Ambiguous' describes something unclear or open to more than one interpretation.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the underlined word: 'The soldiers showed great TENACITY during the siege.'
options: Persistence in the face of difficulty
questions.explanation: 'Tenacity' means firmness of purpose, persisting despite difficulty.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the underlined word: 'The scientist's theory was later VINDICATED.'
questions.explanation: To be 'vindicated' is to be shown or proved to be right after doubt or criticism.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the underlined word: 'She has an INSATIABLE appetite for knowledge.'
questions.explanation: 'Insatiable' describes a desire or appetite that can never be satisfied.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the underlined word: 'The manager's tone during the meeting was CONCILIATORY.'
questions.explanation: A 'conciliatory' tone is one intended to placate or reduce hostility, ending a disagreement.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the underlined word: 'The report contained several PERTINENT facts.'
options: Relevant to the matter at hand
questions.explanation: 'Pertinent' means relevant or applicable to the particular matter under discussion.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the option opposite in meaning to the underlined word: 'The witness gave a very CREDIBLE account.'
questions.explanation: 'Credible' means believable; its opposite is 'unbelievable', meaning hard to accept as true.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the option opposite in meaning to the underlined word: 'The company's charges were considered EXORBITANT.'
questions.explanation: 'Exorbitant' means unreasonably high; its opposite is 'reasonable', meaning fair or moderate.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the option opposite in meaning to the underlined word: 'His statement was completely TRANSPARENT.'
questions.explanation: 'Transparent' means easy to see through or understand; its opposite is 'obscure', meaning unclear or hidden.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the option opposite in meaning to the underlined word: 'The team displayed remarkable COHESION.'
questions.explanation: 'Cohesion' means unity and togetherness; its opposite is 'disunity', meaning a lack of agreement or unity.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the option opposite in meaning to the underlined word: 'The old bridge was considered ROBUST.'
questions.explanation: 'Robust' means strong and sturdy; its opposite is 'fragile', meaning easily broken or weak.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the option opposite in meaning to the underlined word: 'Her explanation of the process was very SUCCINCT.'
questions.explanation: 'Succinct' means expressed briefly and clearly; its opposite is 'long-winded', meaning excessively wordy.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the option opposite in meaning to the underlined word: 'The rebels showed BELLIGERENT intentions.'
questions.explanation: 'Belligerent' means hostile and aggressive; its opposite is 'peaceful', meaning calm and non-violent.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the option opposite in meaning to the underlined word: 'The professor's teaching method was quite ORTHODOX.'
questions.explanation: 'Orthodox' means conventional or traditional; its opposite is 'unconventional', meaning not following usual practice.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the option opposite in meaning to the underlined word: 'The suspect's alibi was VERIFIABLE.'
questions.explanation: 'Verifiable' means capable of being checked or proved true; its opposite is 'unprovable', meaning it cannot be confirmed.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the option opposite in meaning to the underlined word: 'The new employee was remarkably DILIGENT.'
questions.explanation: 'Diligent' means showing careful and persistent effort; its opposite is 'lazy', meaning unwilling to work hard.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the option that best completes the sentence: 'Neither of the answers ___ correct.'
questions.explanation: 'Neither of' takes a singular verb in formal usage, since it refers to each one individually, so 'is' is correct.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the option that best completes the sentence: 'By the time we arrived, the meeting ___ already started.'
questions.explanation: The past perfect 'had started' is used because the meeting started before another past action (our arrival).

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the option that best completes the sentence: 'Of the two candidates, she is the ___ qualified.'
questions.explanation: When comparing exactly two things, the comparative form 'more' is used rather than the superlative 'most'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the option that best completes the sentence: '___ you finish your assignment, you may go out to play.'
questions.explanation: 'Once' correctly introduces a condition that, when completed, permits the following action.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the option that best completes the sentence: 'The chairman, along with the committee members, ___ arriving shortly.'
questions.explanation: Phrases beginning with 'along with' do not change the number of the subject; the singular subject 'the chairman' takes the singular verb 'is'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the option that best completes the sentence: 'I would have attended the ceremony if I ___ informed earlier.'
questions.explanation: This third conditional sentence requires the past perfect 'had been' in the if-clause to describe an unreal past condition.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the option that best completes the sentence: 'He is one of the students who ___ always punctual.'
questions.explanation: The relative clause 'who are always punctual' refers back to 'students' (plural), so the plural verb 'are' is required.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the option that best completes the sentence: 'There ___ several reasons for the delay.'
questions.explanation: The subject following 'there' is the plural noun 'reasons', so the plural verb 'are' is correct.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the option that best completes the sentence: 'She prefers tea ___ coffee.'
questions.explanation: 'Prefer' is idiomatically followed by 'to' when comparing two things, as in 'prefer tea to coffee.'

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the option that best completes the sentence: 'The twins look so alike that I can hardly tell one ___ the other.'
questions.explanation: The idiomatic expression 'tell one from the other' uses the preposition 'from' to indicate distinguishing between things.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the option that best completes the sentence: 'He apologized ___ arriving late.'
questions.explanation: 'Apologize for' is the standard prepositional pairing used when expressing regret for an action.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the option that best completes the sentence: 'This is the house ___ I was born.'
questions.explanation: 'Where' is the correct relative adverb to introduce a clause describing a place.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the option that best completes the sentence: 'Hardly ___ the plane landed when it began to rain heavily.'
questions.explanation: The construction 'hardly...when' requires the past perfect 'had landed' to describe one past event immediately followed by another.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the option that best completes the sentence: 'The book, as well as the notebooks, ___ on the table.'
questions.explanation: 'As well as' does not change the number of the subject; the singular subject 'the book' takes the singular verb 'is'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the option that best completes the sentence: 'Scarcely ___ she entered the room when the phone rang.'
questions.explanation: The construction 'scarcely...when' requires the past perfect 'had entered' to show one action closely followed by another.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the option that best completes the sentence: 'It is high time we ___ this matter seriously.'
questions.explanation: After the expression 'it is high time', the past tense form ('took') is used to express that an action is overdue.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the option that best completes the sentence: 'The chief guest, together with his aides, ___ expected at noon.'
questions.explanation: 'Together with' does not alter subject number; the singular subject 'the chief guest' takes the singular verb 'is'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the option that best completes the sentence: 'Not until the results were released ___ the truth known.'
questions.explanation: The negative adverbial 'not until' at the start of the sentence triggers subject-verb inversion, giving 'was the truth known.'

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the option that best completes the sentence: 'She is used ___ working long hours.'
questions.explanation: 'Used to' followed by a gerund ('working') describes something one is accustomed to doing.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the option that best completes the sentence: 'The teacher insisted that every student ___ present.'
questions.explanation: After verbs like 'insist' expressing a demand, the subjunctive base form 'be' is used regardless of subject.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Identify the figure of speech used: 'The wind whispered through the trees.'
questions.explanation: Giving the wind the human ability to 'whisper' is an example of personification.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Identify the figure of speech used: 'Her smile was as bright as the sun.'
questions.explanation: This comparison uses 'as...as' to directly liken two things, which is the defining feature of a simile.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Identify the figure of speech used: 'He is the black sheep of the family.'
questions.explanation: Calling a person 'the black sheep' directly, without using 'like' or 'as', is a metaphor implying he is seen as different or disgraced.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Identify the figure of speech used: 'The thunder roared angrily across the sky.'
questions.explanation: Describing thunder as 'roaring angrily' gives it a human emotion, which is personification.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Identify the figure of speech used: 'I've told you a million times to clean your room.'
questions.explanation: 'A million times' is a deliberate exaggeration for emphasis, which is the defining feature of hyperbole.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Identify the figure of speech used: 'The silence was deafening.'
questions.explanation: 'Deafening silence' combines two contradictory terms, making it an oxymoron.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Identify the figure of speech used: 'Peter Piper picked a peck of pickled peppers.'
questions.explanation: The repetition of the initial 'p' sound across neighbouring words is alliteration.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Identify the figure of speech used: 'The bee buzzed lazily in the summer heat.'
questions.explanation: 'Buzzed' imitates the actual sound a bee makes, which is onomatopoeia.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Identify the figure of speech used: 'All the world's a stage, and all the men and women merely players.'
questions.explanation: This line directly equates the world with a stage and people with players, without using 'like' or 'as', making it a metaphor.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Identify the figure of speech used: 'The car screeched to a halt.'
questions.explanation: 'Screeched' imitates the actual sound produced by the car's tyres, which is onomatopoeia.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the idiom: 'She only visits her hometown ONCE IN A BLUE MOON.'
questions.explanation: 'Once in a blue moon' is an idiom meaning something that happens very rarely.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the option that best explains the proverb: 'A stitch in time saves nine.'
options: Acting promptly prevents a bigger problem later
Time cannot be saved once lost
Nine is always better than one
It is best to sew clothes at night
questions.explanation: The proverb means that dealing with a small problem promptly can prevent it from becoming a much bigger one.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the option that best explains the proverb: 'Actions speak louder than words.'
options: Words are more powerful than actions
Silence is always the best response
Loud voices are more persuasive than quiet ones
What a person does matters more than what they say
questions.explanation: The proverb means that a person's deeds reveal their true character or intentions more than their promises.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the idiom: 'The manager decided to LET SLEEPING DOGS LIE.'
options: Adopt several pet dogs at once
Report the matter to the police immediately
Wake his staff early every morning
Avoid interfering in a situation that could cause trouble
questions.explanation: 'Let sleeping dogs lie' means to deliberately avoid interfering in a situation that is currently calm, so as not to cause trouble.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the idiom: 'The host told a joke to BREAK THE ICE at the party.'
questions.explanation: 'Break the ice' means to initiate conversation and relieve tension or awkwardness in a social situation.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the idiom: 'By carpooling, they managed to KILL TWO BIRDS WITH ONE STONE.'
options: Accomplish two things with a single action
questions.explanation: 'Kill two birds with one stone' means to achieve two objectives through a single action.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the idiom: 'His constant lateness was THE LAST STRAW for the supervisor.'
options: The beginning of a new working relationship
A pleasant surprise for the supervisor
The final problem that leads to a loss of patience
The most minor of several complaints
questions.explanation: 'The last straw' refers to the final small problem in a series that finally causes someone to lose patience or give up.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the idiom: 'Under pressure from the journalists, he finally SPILLED THE BEANS.'
questions.explanation: 'Spill the beans' is an idiom meaning to reveal secret or confidential information.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the option that best explains the proverb: 'Every cloud has a silver lining.'
options: Even difficult situations have some positive aspect
Silver is more valuable than gold

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text:
Across Nigeria, an increasing number of households and small businesses are turning to solar power as a reliable alternative to the epileptic supply from the national grid. Solar panels, once considered a luxury reserved for the wealthy, have become more affordable in recent years as manufacturing costs have fallen and local assemblers have entered the market. For many shop owners in urban centres, a modest solar installation now means they no longer have to shut down operations whenever grid power fails, nor must they spend heavily on diesel to run noisy generators. In rural areas without any grid connection at all, small solar home systems have allowed families to light their homes, charge mobile phones, and, in some cases, power a small refrigerator to preserve food and medicine. Even so, the initial cost of a solar system capable of powering an entire home remains beyond the reach of many low-income families, and the batteries used to store solar energy still need periodic, and often expensive, replacement. Government incentives and cheaper financing options, experts argue, will be needed if solar power is to move from being a supplement for the well-off to a genuine, widespread substitute for unreliable grid electricity.

According to the passage, why are households and small businesses turning to solar power?
options: Because the government has banned diesel generators
Because solar panels are cheaper than candles
As a reliable alternative to the unreliable national grid supply
Because banks now require it for loan approval
questions.explanation: The passage states people are 'turning to solar power as a reliable alternative to the epileptic supply from the national grid.'

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text:
Educators across Nigeria have expressed growing concern over what many describe as a decline in the reading culture among young people. A generation ago, it was common to see students engrossed in novels during holidays or exchanging paperbacks with classmates; today, many of the same students spend their free hours scrolling through short videos and social media posts instead. Some teachers argue that this shift is not simply a matter of laziness but reflects how thoroughly digital platforms have been designed to capture and hold attention in ways that a printed page cannot easily compete with. Others are less pessimistic, pointing out that many young Nigerians now read constantly, just in different formats: text messages, online articles, and e-books accessed through their phones. What worries literacy experts most, however, is not the format but the depth of engagement, since scrolling quickly through short posts trains the mind for brevity rather than the sustained concentration that a full-length novel or textbook demands. Without deliberate effort by parents and schools to encourage longer, more focused reading, they warn, students may increasingly struggle with the kind of extended comprehension that examinations and university study still require.

What concern have educators expressed, according to the passage?
options: A decline in the reading culture among young people
A shortage of textbooks in secondary schools
An increase in the price of paperback books
A rise in the number of students reading novels
questions.explanation: The passage opens by noting 'growing concern over what many describe as a decline in the reading culture among young people.'
